did_you_know.text: Jeremiah describes Judah’s sin as something engraved deeply: with an iron stylus and a flint point, it is carved on the tablet of the heart and on the horns of the altars. The image emphasizes the depth of the sin and its connection with altar worship.
The chapter warns against relying on human beings alone: anyone who makes flesh his strength and turns his heart away from the LORD is described as “cursed.”

A person who trusts in human beings alone is compared to a solitary plant in a dry and salty land, which does not see prosperity when it comes. This is an image of life without a stable source of security.

In contrast to the “cursed man,” the person who trusts in the LORD is described as “blessed,” with the LORD himself as his source of security. This presents a choice between relying solely on human strength and trusting in the LORD.

The person who trusts in the LORD is compared to a tree planted near water: even in heat and drought, it remains fresh and does not stop producing fruit. The image emphasizes stability and the ability to remain productive in difficult conditions.
The verse, “The heart is deceitful above all things,” presents the human heart as deceptive and incurably sick. Therefore, people cannot always rely on their own understanding of their motives.

According to the chapter, the LORD searches the heart and examines the mind, and he repays each person according to his ways and the fruit of his deeds. Moral responsibility is therefore judged by actions, not only by declared intentions.

The chapter compares wealth gained dishonestly to a bird that sits on eggs it did not lay: just as something like this does not turn out as it should, such wealth may be abandoned halfway through life and prove to be empty.

Jeremiah calls the LORD “the hope of Israel” and “the fountain of living water,” while describing those who forsake him as those who will be written in the earth. The contrast presents the LORD as the source of hope and life.

In the final section of the chapter, Jeremiah is commanded to stand at the gates of Jerusalem and proclaim the warning about the Sabbath to everyone who enters and leaves, including the kings of Judah and the people of the city.
The central prohibition in the Sabbath prophecy is carrying a load and doing work on the Sabbath, along with the command to make the day holy, as the ancestors were instructed.

The prophecy presents Sabbath observance as the condition for Jerusalem’s blessed future: kings, officials, residents, pilgrims, and those bringing sacrifices will enter through its gates. If they do not listen, fire will consume the city’s palaces.
